a: He will wash a soul clean of its sins
p: Swete's Greek reads "in sins", and his note gives no other reading. The Plain English Translation follows Gray's correction, "from sins".

readings.w: Gray's correction (no Greek manuscript); the Syriac, as Gray gives it, has "the sins of" a soul
readings.en: he will cleanse a soul from sins
readings.plain: He will wash a soul clean of its sins

readings.w: Swete's text; his note lists no other Greek reading
readings.en: he will cleanse in sins a soul
readings.plain: He will wash a soul clean in its sins

why: "Cleanse in sins" gives poor sense. Gray translates "from sins", compares 10:1 ("to be cleansed from sin"), and explains the Greek as a Hebrew mem ("from") read as bet ("in"), "a frequent error". The Syriac also makes the sins what is washed away. The Plain English Translation follows that sense and leaves Swete's text here.

a: With hymns. Of Solomon.
p: Swete prints "In hymns", from one manuscript; the others have "A hymn".

readings.w: Swete's text, with the manuscript he calls r (Gray's R)
readings.plain: With hymns. Of Solomon.

readings.w: The other manuscripts in Swete's note (c, h, i, l, p, v; Gray: J, L, C, H)
readings.plain: A hymn of Solomon.

why: The site's base text is Swete's, and the heading changes no meaning. Most manuscripts read "A hymn", as in 14:0 and 16:0.
b: Names of the witnesses in this part. Swete calls his manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p, r and v; Gray calls his R, J, L, C and H. Neither book, in the pages read for this site, gives a key from one set to the other. The Gray letters in brackets in these entries are this site's inference from readings the two agree on: r = R, i = J, c = C, l = L, and Gray's H standing for h, usually together with m, p and v. The match does not hold everywhere: at 15:9 and 16:1 the two notes disagree about l and h (see those entries).

a: he will not bend them out of shape by his discipline
p: Swete prints diaprepsei; every other manuscript in his note has diastrepsei, "twist". The Plain English Translation follows the others.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete lists (c, h, i, l, m, p, v); Ryle and James's text
readings.en: and he will not pervert (them) in discipline
readings.plain: he will not bend them out of shape by his discipline

readings.w: Swete's text (with r)
readings.en: and he will not be conspicuous (or: make a show) in discipline
readings.plain: he will not make a show of them by his discipline

why: Diaprepō means "to stand out" and gives poor sense after "he will make straight the paths". Diastrephō, "to twist", is the natural opposite of "make straight", is read by all the other manuscripts Swete lists, and is printed by Ryle and James; Gray's "doth not pervert" also follows it. The Plain English Translation also leaves Swete's printed text at 9:12, 17:16 and 18:4; each has its own entry.

a: to bring lasting soundness of mind
p: Most manuscripts read sōphrosynē, "soundness of mind"; three have euphrosynē, "gladness".

readings.w: Swete's text, with h, m, p, r, v
readings.plain: to bring lasting soundness of mind

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls c, i, l; Ryle and James; Gray
readings.plain: to bring lasting gladness

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's printed text, though "soundness of mind" is an odd goal for salvation. "Gladness" may well be original: it fits 10:6-7, where Israel praises "with gladness", and Isaiah 35:10. The two Greek words differ by two letters.

a: Like a fire among a people that sets their beauty ablaze
t: A fire among a people, or on a threshing floor?
p: Most witnesses compare the slanderer to a fire burning a people's beauty; one group has a fire burning stubble on a threshing floor.

readings.w: Swete's text, with c, i, l, r (Gray: R, J, L, C, and the Syriac in substance)
readings.orig: ὥσπερ ἐν λαῷ πῦρ ἀνάπτον καλλονὴν αὐτοῦ
readings.en: as among a people a fire burning up its beauty
readings.plain: Like a fire among a people that sets their beauty ablaze

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, v for "threshing floor" (p has a third form, allō, "another"), and h, m, p, v for "stubble" (Gray: H)
readings.orig: ὥσπερ ἐν ἅλῳ πῦρ ἀνάπτον καλάμην αὐτοῦ
readings.en: as on a threshing floor a fire burning up its stubble
readings.plain: Like a fire on a threshing floor that sets its stubble ablaze

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete and the larger group. Gray judged the threshing-floor reading improbable, though Ryle and James built their rendering on it. Gray doubts that either reading recovers the original.

a: The ungodly man was shaken
p: All manuscripts read "the ungodly". Several scholars change it to "the righteous" to fit the context.

readings.w: All Greek manuscripts and the Syriac (Gray); Swete's text
readings.plain: The ungodly man was shaken

readings.w: Conjecture of Wellhausen, von Gebhardt and Kittel, adopted by Gray (no manuscript)
readings.plain: The righteous man was shaken

why: The Plain English Translation follows the manuscripts. The conjecture makes good sense, since 13:5-7 speaks of the righteous, but no witness has it. Gray's English, the main public-domain translation, adopts it, so readers comparing translations will meet it.

a: A new psalm with a song from a glad heart
t: A new psalm, or a psalm and praise?
p: Most manuscripts read kainon, "new"; one group reads kai ainon, "and praise".

readings.w: Swete's text, with i, l, r (Gray: J, R, L and the Syriac)
readings.plain: A new psalm with a song from a glad heart

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p, v (Gray: H)
readings.plain: A psalm and praise with a song from a glad heart

why: The two readings differ only by where the letters are divided. "A new psalm" has the better support and echoes the Psalter's "new song" (Psalm 96:1).

a: they will run from the devout like people chased in war
t: Chased in war, or by famine?
p: Swete prints von Gebhardt's conjecture "(chased) in war". The manuscripts have "from famine" or "famine", which make little sense.

readings.w: Swete's text: von Gebhardt's conjecture, as Swete's note marks it
readings.plain: they will run from the devout like people chased in war

readings.w: The manuscript Swete calls i (Gray: J)
readings.plain: they will run from the devout like people chased off by famine

readings.w: The manuscript Swete calls r (Gray: R)
readings.en: as of one pursued from famine
readings.plain: they will run from the devout like someone chased off by famine

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls c, h, m, p, v (Gray: C, H)
readings.en: as of one pursued of famine
readings.plain: they will run from the devout like someone hunted by famine

why: Gray says the manuscript readings "yield no tolerable sense", since famine is itself one of the plagues that flee (15:8). The conjecture fits 15:9d, "as if by enemies trained for war". Swete printed it, and the Plain English Translation follows Swete, with this entry to show that no manuscript has it. The Greek of the manuscript readings is put together from two separate items in Swete's note (diōkomenou in c, h, m, p, r, v; apo limou in i, r; limou alone in c, h, l, m, p, v). Swete's note does not list l for diōkomenou, while Gray gives that form to L.

a: when God visits the earth with his judgment.
p: Four manuscripts add "to repay sinners for all time". The same four lack the last line of 15:15 (see there).

readings.w: Swete's text, with c, i, l, r
readings.orig: ὅταν ἐπισκέπτηται ὁ θεὸς τὴν γῆν ἐν κρίματι αὐτοῦ
readings.en: when God visits the earth in his judgment
readings.plain: when God visits the earth with his judgment.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p, v (Gray: H)
readings.orig: ὅταν ἐπισκέπτηται ὁ θεὸς τὴν γῆν ἐν κρίματι αὐτοῦ, ἀποδοῦναι ἁμαρτωλοῖς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα χρόνον
readings.en: when God visits the earth in his judgment, to repay sinners forever
readings.plain: when God visits the earth with his judgment, / to pay sinners back for all time.

why: The longer text moves the closing line of 15:15 up into 15:14 in a new form. The Plain English Translation follows Swete and the larger group. This entry goes with the one at 15:15.

a: And the sinners will be destroyed for all time.
p: Four manuscripts lack this line; they have a different line after 15:14 instead. Goes with the entry at 15:14.

readings.w: Swete's text, with c, i, l, r
readings.orig: καὶ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀπολοῦνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα χρόνον
readings.en: and sinners will perish for all time
readings.plain: And the sinners will be destroyed for all time.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p, v (Gray: H omits)

why: As at 15:14: the Plain English Translation follows Swete and the larger group.

a: falling heavy with sleep
t: Heavy sleep or decay of sleep?
p: Swete prints kataphora, "a falling" (heavy drowsiness). Five manuscripts have kataphthora, "ruin", which Gray thinks meant "the pit".

readings.w: Swete's text, with h, p, r (the manuscripts his note does not list for the other reading); Gray gives it from R and L
readings.plain: falling heavy with sleep

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls c, i, l, m, v; Gray gives it from J, C, H, and the Syriac has "sleep of corruption"
readings.plain: falling into the ruin of sleep

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. Gray argues that kataphthora was the original Greek and stood for Hebrew shachat, "pit", as in the Greek of Psalm 49:9, with "of sleep" a gloss; on his view the line read "I had all but slipped down to the pit". Here the two notes do not match: Swete gives kataphthora to l and not to h, while Gray gives kataphora to L and kataphthora to H. The conflict is not resolved (see the entry at 10:0).

a: Keep the work of my hands straight in your place
t: In your place, in your pattern, or before you?
p: Swete prints topō, "place"; Gray says all manuscripts but one have typō, "pattern", and thinks the original was "before you".

readings.w: Swete's text; Gray reports it from J
readings.plain: Keep the work of my hands straight in your place

readings.w: All other Greek manuscripts (Gray)
readings.plain: Keep the work of my hands straight by your pattern

readings.w: The Syriac, as Gray reads it; his suggested original
readings.plain: Keep the work of my hands straight before you

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. Gray's explanation, that both Greek readings grew from enōpion sou, "before you", is attractive, but no Greek manuscript has it.

a: is over the nations forever
p: Swete follows one manuscript; all the others add "in judgment".

readings.w: Swete's text, with r
readings.orig: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ἐπὶ τὰ ἔθνη
readings.plain: is over the nations forever

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, i, l, m, p, v; Gray
readings.orig: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ἐπὶ τὰ ἔθνη ἐν κρίσει
readings.en: forever over the nations in judgment
readings.plain: is over the nations forever, in judgment

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. Gray translates "in judgement" and explains the pair: "Mercy for Israel; judgement for the nations" (17:3-4).

a: They laid waste David's throne in the arrogance of their exchange.
p: Swete's allagmatos is "exchange"; four manuscripts have alalagmatos, "war cry".

readings.w: Swete's text, with i, l, r (Gray: R, J, L, "in pride of price")
readings.plain: They laid waste David's throne in the arrogance of their exchange.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p, v (Gray: H)
readings.plain: They laid waste David's throne in arrogant uproar.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete and the larger group. Gray prefers "tumultuous arrogance" and calls "in pride of price" "senseless"; read as "exchange", the phrase can mean the swap of David's line for their own (17:7).

a: God will not have mercy on them.
p: Six manuscripts begin "according to their deeds", and four of those lack the "not": "God will have mercy on them."

readings.w: Swete's text, with r (Gray: R and the Syriac lack "according to their deeds")
readings.en: God will not have mercy on them
readings.plain: God will not have mercy on them.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls i, l
readings.orig: κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν οὐκ ἐλεήσει αὐτοὺς ὁ θεός
readings.en: according to their works God will not have mercy on them
readings.plain: According to their deeds God will not have mercy on them.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p, v (Gray: H); Ryle and James's text
readings.orig: κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν ἐλεήσει αὐτοὺς ὁ θεός
readings.en: according to their works God will have mercy on them
readings.plain: According to their deeds God will have mercy on them.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete and r. Gray explains "according to their deeds" here as a copyist's repetition of the same words at the end of 17:10, and says that in H the negative "has been lost"; his translation reads "God showed them no pity". The negative fits the next line, where God hunts down their offspring. Ryle and James printed the reading without "not" ("According to their works God will have mercy upon them") and weighed two senses: ironic (his "mercy" matches their evil deeds, so he punishes them) or plain (he spares whatever good he finds). They preferred the plain sense and linked it to Pompey's leaving Hyrcanus II as high priest.

a: The lawless one emptied our land
t: The lawless one or the wind?
p: Three manuscripts read anomos, "lawless one"; four read anemos, "wind".

readings.w: Swete's text, with i, l, r (Gray: R, J, L and the Syriac)
readings.plain: The lawless one emptied our land

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p, v (Gray: H "the tempest")
readings.plain: The wind emptied our land

why: The lawless one fits 17:14-15, which speak of a person with a heart "foreign to our God". The Syriac agrees, and Gray follows it. The two Greek words differ by one letter.

a: what the nations do for their gods
p: Swete prints r's tous theous, "the gods". The other six manuscripts have tois theois, "for the gods", whose sense the Plain English Translation gives.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, i, l, m, p, v (Gray: J, L, H, and the Syriac)
readings.orig: καθὼς καὶ τὰ ἔθνη ἐν ταῖς πόλεσι τοῖς θεοῖς αὐτῶν
readings.en: as also the nations in the cities for their gods
readings.plain: what the nations do for their gods

readings.w: Swete's text, with r (Gray: R)
readings.orig: καθὼς καὶ τὰ ἔθνη ἐν ταῖς πόλεσι τοὺς θεοὺς αὐτῶν
readings.en: as also the nations in the cities their gods
readings.plain: what the nations do their gods

why: Gray judged R's accusative "unintelligible, but probably earlier", and the dative a substitute for it. The accusative gives no clear sense in English, so the Plain English Translation follows the dative here and leaves Swete's text. See the note on this verse.

a: Those who loved the assemblies of the devout ran away from them.
p: This line repeats 17:18. Only the manuscript Swete calls r has it here; the six others his note cites lack it.

readings.w: Swete's text, with r
readings.orig: ἐφύγοσαν ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν οἱ ἀγαπῶντες συναγωγὰς ὁσίων
readings.en: those who loved the assemblies of the devout fled from them
readings.plain: Those who loved the assemblies of the devout ran away from them.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, i, l, m, p, v (his notes on Psalm 17 do not cite c)

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text, which keeps the line. It is probably a copyist's repetition of 17:18; Gray's translation leaves it out.

a: and their king will be the Lord Messiah
p: The manuscripts read christos kyrios, "Messiah, Lord". Many scholars think the original meant "the Lord's Messiah".

readings.w: Swete's text and the manuscripts that have the clause; the Syriac (Gray)
readings.plain: and their king will be the Lord Messiah

readings.w: Proposed sense (Ewald, Hilgenfeld, Geiger, Carrière, Vernes, Wellhausen, Robertson Smith and others, as Ryle and James list them; most kept the Greek and called it a mistranslation; Gray's "the anointed of the Lord"); no manuscript
readings.en: and their king (is) the Lord's Messiah
readings.plain: and their king will be the Lord's Messiah

why: Every witness that has the clause reads kyrios. Most of those who prefer "the Lord's Messiah" did not change the Greek; they held that the translator rendered a Hebrew meshiach YHWH, "the LORD's anointed", as the Greek of Lamentations 4:20 also does, and that the original meant that. Ryle and James thought the Greek might be a correct rendering of a Hebrew adon, "lord", a title fit for a human king, and rejected the idea of a Christian change because this is the only phrase in the book ever suspected. The Plain English Translation follows the Greek as transmitted and gives the alternative here.
b: The manuscript Swete calls i lacks the whole clause "for all of them will be holy, and their king will be the Lord Messiah". The same two words christos kyrios stand in Luke 2:11, which the site renders "Messiah and Lord". In 18:0 and 18:8 the genitive christou kyriou is "the Lord's Messiah".

a: For he will shatter the earth by the word of his mouth forever.
p: Two manuscripts read kataxei, "he will shatter"; five read pataxei, "he will strike", the verb of the Greek of Isaiah 11:4.

readings.w: Swete's text, with i, r
readings.plain: For he will shatter the earth by the word of his mouth forever.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, l, m, p, v; the Greek of Isaiah 11:4
readings.plain: For he will strike the earth by the word of his mouth forever.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. "Strike" may be the original, since the line quotes Isaiah 11:4 (Swete's Septuagint reads pataxei gēn tō logō tou stomatos autou); it may also be a copyist's correction toward Isaiah. Gray renders "smite".

a: so that he can rule great peoples
t: Great peoples or a great people?
p: Swete follows one manuscript in the plural; the others have the singular, "a great people".

readings.w: Swete's text, with r
readings.plain: so that he can rule great peoples

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, i, l, m, p, v; Gray
readings.plain: so that he can rule a great people

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. The singular would mean Israel; the plural would include the nations he rules (17:32).

a: He will lead them all as equals
p: Three witnesses read isotēti, "equality"; four, with the text of one more, read hosiotēti, "holiness".

readings.w: Swete's text, with i, r and the margin of l (Gray: R, J, L margin)
readings.plain: He will lead them all as equals

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p, v and the text of l (Gray: L text, H); Ryle and James's text
readings.plain: He will lead them all in holiness

why: "Equality" is the less expected word and fits the next line, where no one is oppressed. "Holiness" could be a copyist's change to the book's familiar word.

a: A psalm of Solomon. Again, of the Lord's Messiah.
p: Two manuscripts read eti, "again"; four read epi, "about".

readings.w: Swete's text, with i, r (Gray: R, J)
readings.plain: A psalm of Solomon. Again, of the Lord's Messiah.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, l, p, v (Gray: L, H)
readings.plain: A psalm of Solomon. About the Lord's Messiah.

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. "Again" links Psalm 18 to Psalm 17, the other psalm of the Messiah.

a: You discipline us
p: Swete prints r's spelling paidia. The other six manuscripts have paideia, "discipline", which the Plain English Translation follows.

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, i, l, m, p, v; Gray ("Thy chastisement")
readings.plain: You discipline us

readings.w: Swete's text, with r
readings.en: your paidia (is) on us (the same phrase, spelled with one letter fewer)
readings.plain: Your paidia is on us

why: The two spellings differ by one letter. The book's own word for discipline is spelled paideia elsewhere (13:8; 18:8, "the rod of discipline"), and the verse goes on to a father training his firstborn, so the Plain English Translation reads "discipline" with the other manuscripts and Gray, and leaves Swete's spelling here.

a: to set them all before the Lord
t: Before the Lord, or in the Lord's fear?
p: Two manuscripts read enōpion, "before"; four read en phobō, "in the fear (of)".

readings.w: Swete's text, with l, r
readings.en: to set them all before the Lord
readings.plain: to set them all before the Lord

readings.w: The manuscripts Swete calls h, m, p, v; Ryle and James's text
readings.orig: καταστῆσαι πάντας αὐτοὺς ἐν φόβῳ κυρίου
readings.en: to set them all in the fear of the Lord
readings.plain: to set them all in the fear of the Lord

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete. "In the fear" repeats the phrase of 18:7-10 and may have come in from there.
